text: The message arrived on a Tuesday, written on paper that smelled faintly of thunderstorms.
Nobody remembered who had first suggested we open the door in the basement, only that we had all agreed it was a good idea.
The town's only traffic light had been stuck on yellow for as long as anyone could recall.
She found the key taped to the underside of a park bench, exactly where the fortune cookie had promised.
The elevator always skipped the seventh floor, unless you were carrying an umbrella.
Our cat started bringing home small objects that did not belong to any of our neighbors.
The lighthouse keeper quit the same week the ships stopped needing lighthouses.
Every mirror in the house agreed on the weather except the one in the guest bathroom.
The recipe card was written in handwriting that matched nobody who had ever lived in the house.
We agreed to split the bill evenly, which is how we learned who had ordered the invisible dessert.
The train was late, but the conductor insisted we were exactly on time according to a clock only he could see.
The library's lost-and-found box had grown large enough to require its own shelf.
He introduced himself as the substitute teacher for a class that had never existed on the schedule.
The dog barked once at the empty corner, then sat down as if waiting for an answer.
Someone had replaced every photograph in the album with versions where we were all smiling a little too widely.
The vending machine offered a button labeled "Surprise" and no change slot.
The old radio picked up a station that only played songs from birthdays we had not had yet.
We found footprints in the attic dust leading toward a wall with no door.
The coffee shop began spelling everyone's name correctly, which made people more nervous than the mistakes ever had.
The fortune read, "You will soon meet someone who remembers your middle name," and I do not have a middle name.
The office plant died the day we finally fixed the leaky ceiling.
The GPS insisted the fastest route was through a field that had not been a road since before cars existed.
Every clock in the museum stopped at 3:17 except the sundial.
The invitation said "formal attire" and included a diagram of a constellation nobody recognized.
The beach was crowded, but the footprints in the wet sand only ever showed one direction.
The hotel keycard worked on every door except the one with our room number on it.
The choir director asked us to hum the note we heard in our dreams, and the room went silent in twelve different keys.
The package was addressed to someone who had moved out three tenants ago, with postage dated next month.
The campfire story ended exactly where it had started, which we assumed was a joke until morning.
The last page of the diary was blank except for a single sentence written in ink that was still wet.
